Items.Authors: Prakriti Gupta, Yashvi Sharma, John I. Bailey
Items.Title: ZShooter: ScopeSim and early data reduction prototyping to enhance design
Items.Abstract: We are building a ZShooter‑specific extension of the ScopeSim instrument‑simulation framework and coupling it to existing open‑source echelle pipelines such as PyReduce and PypeIt. This end‑to‑end setup produces realistic detector‑level frames for the three‑arm ZSpec spectrograph and tri‑band ZImager camera and immediately feeds them into prototype reduction recipes. Here we will demonstrate how this approach lets a small team explore performance trades, observing strategies, and calibration plans very early in the design, while simultaneously de‑risking the future data‑reduction pipeline and quick‑look tools.

Items.Authors: Pontsho L. Maruping
Items.Title: Big telescopes, real communities: maintaining a “social licence to operate” through MeerKAT to SKA
Items.Abstract: World-class telescopes don’t succeed on engineering alone. For facilities built to operate for decades, scientific output depends on stable site access, predictable operations, and trusted relationships with host communities. The people need to feel respected, heard, and able to share in the benefits. Drawing on SARAO’s experience building and operating MeerKAT and participating in construction of the SKA, this talk distils practical ways to earn and sustain a “social licence to operate”. It covers continuous engagement with visible feedback loops; clear communication about constraints and trade-offs; fair, auditable local procurement and supplier development; skills pathways that convert training into real work; and accessible mechanisms to resolve concerns when they arise. The talk closes with lessons learned about expectation management through various phases, from construction, operations, and expansion in order to maintain trust and treat community partnership as an operational KPI, not a communications exercise.

Items.Authors: Shawn D. Domagal-Goldman
Items.Title: NASA’s flagship observatories: from Hubble to the Habitable Worlds Observatory
Items.Abstract: This talk will discuss the Habitable Worlds Observatory, in the context of the flagship missions that have come before it, including the Hubble Space Telescope, the Chandra X-ray Observatory, the James Webb Space Telescope, and the soon-to-launch Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. HWO will continue the tradition of these missions to pursue big-picture questions only they can answer, while they advance questions across astrophysics. HWO will pursue multiple big-picture questions related to how the universe works, how it evolved over time, and whether it hosts biopsheres other than our own. That last question is also the driver of many of the mission’s technical tall poles, which will be discussed along with our plans to overcome those challenges.

Items.Authors: Peter G. Tuthill
Items.Title: Astrometric detection of rocky exoplanets from inexpensive space platforms
Items.Abstract: The detection of exoplanets by way of astrometric monitoring of the host star to reveal gravitational reflex motion requires extreme precision in measurement stability for Earth-mass objects. Despite this, astrometry is widely regarded as the most promising technology for the most desired of all targets: true Earth analogues in the solar neighbourhood. Formerly thought to require flagship class investment, recently several smaller concepts such as the TOLIMAN and SHERA missions have shown that detections are possible, at least in principle, from more modest space platforms. A key enabling feature of these missions is narrow-angle astrometry: a binary star provides its own astrometric reference greatly alleviating problems from using distant, faint field stars. However, few nearby star systems are multiple. This paper advances novel optical concepts featuring ultra-stable telescopes of modest (<0.5m) aperture for micro-arcsecond monitoring of isolated single stars.

Items.Authors: Ryan Griffiths, Siddharth Maharana, Matthias Tecza
Items.Title: Comparing the contrast performance of two IFU technologies for exoplanet direct imaging with ELT-PCS
Items.Abstract: The Planetary Camera and Spectrograph (PCS) is an upcoming, dedicated high-contrast imager for the Extremely Large Telescope. The primary goal of PCS is to leverage the resolution provided by the ELT to image rocky exoplanets around nearby stars, requiring an instrument contrast exceeding that of any existing direct imager. The choice of integral field unit (IFU) for PCS must therefore maximise the contrast delivered by the science instrument, and synergise effectively with post-processing techniques. In this paper, we present a direct comparison of a novel “twisted” image slicer with a lenslet array IFU, made using the Modular Oxford Integral Field Spectrograph. We compare the implemented calibration routines and the radial 5-sigma contrast delivered by each IFU. This will include results with and without post-processing, and in a variety of simulated atmospheric conditions. We discuss the implications of these results for the conceptual design of PCS.

Items.Authors: G. Barbieri Ripamonti, F. Columbro, P. de Bernardis, T. Iida, S. Masi, R. Akizawa, E. Battistelli, M. De Petris, A. Coppolecchia, L. Lamagna, E. Marchitelli, T. Matsumura, M. Najafi, A. Occhiuzzi, H. Ohsaki, S. Okumura, A. Paiella, F. Piacentini, G. Pisano, S. Stellati
Items.Title: Design and performance of a cryogenic polarization modulation unit for CMB experiments
Items.Abstract: The most recent Cosmic Microwave Background surveys aim to detect its extremely faint polarization signal, requiring modulation for clean measurements. We are developing a cryogenic Polarization Modulation Unit (PMU) for the LSPE/SWIPE balloon-borne experiment and the LiteBIRD space mission. The PMU consists of a half-wave plate (HWP) levitating and rotating on a superconducting magnetic bearing (SMB) in a cryogenic environment, driven by an electromagnetic motor. LiteBIRD’s stringent requirements demand a heat load below 7mW and a HWP temperature under 20K. In this work, we present tests performed on the current breadboard model of the rotation mechanism, with the goal of identifying the dominant dissipation mechanisms and evaluating their thermal impact on the rotor. This validated test procedure will be applied to the upgraded PMU currently under development, which features an improved SMB with higher magnetic field homogeneity.

Items.Authors: Norma Hurtado
Items.Title: Differences and similarities of the development phases of ground-based and space-based astronomical instrumentation
Items.Abstract: This paper compares engineering development approaches in space-based and ground-based observatory instrumentation, highlighting how historically distinct processes are converging with the emergence of extremely large telescopes and increasingly complex instruments. The analysis draws on experience from two major projects: METIS, a first-light instrument for ESO’s ELT, and AIRS, the infrared spectrometer for ESA’s ARIEL mission. Through roles in system engineering and project control, and more than 25 years in astronomical institutions, key differences and commonalities are examined in areas such as consortium organization, requirements and documentation management, configuration control, verification planning, model and prototyping strategies, technical readiness levels, maintainability, manufacturing and test readiness reviews, and non-conformity handling. The main goal is to identify areas where cross-domain synergies can be found and methodologies can be effectively transferred.

Items.Authors: Derek Y. Kubo, Ming-Tang Chen, Sally S. M. Lau, Peter Oshiro, Ryan Chilson, Naomi Dunhour-Yuen, Jean-François Cliche, Vadym J. Bidula, Andre Renard, Nina Gusinskaia, Lou-Chien Lu, Yau-De Huang
Items.Title: Front-end signal processing and operational status of the FRB Hawaiʻi outrigger station
Items.Abstract: The FRB array in Pāhala, Hawaiʻi, will operate as an outrigger station for CHIME, providing a ~4,500 km baseline that greatly improves FRB localization. The array includes ten 6-m dishes and twelve log-periodic antennas covering 400–800 MHz, aligned to overlap a portion of CHIME’s sky coverage. Analog signals from each element are continuously digitized and stored in a ring buffer. When CHIME issues an FRB trigger, the Hawaiʻi station saves the relevant data to non-volatile storage for later upload and offline correlation. This paper describes the design and performance of the antennas, LNAs, and fiber-optic links that drive overall system sensitivity, and discusses RFI challenges and mitigation. A companion paper covers the back-end processing system.

Items.Authors: Kristin K. Madsen, Raul Riveros, Kai-Wing Chan, Youwei Yao, william Zhang, Joseph Colosimo, Tabatha DeVita, Naoko Hamaguchi, Michal Hlinka, Steven Kenyon, Richard Koenecke, James Mazzarella, Ai Numata, Takashi Okajima, Jessica Patel, Marton Sharpe, Jonathan Tsang
Items.Title: GSFC's next generation X-ray optics: enabling sub-arcsecond resolution for future missions
Items.Abstract: The Next Generation X-ray Optics (NGXO) team at Goddard Space Flight Center is developing X-ray mirror technology capable of building mirror assemblies for flagship missions like Lynx and Probe missions like AXIS, as well as Explorer missions like STAR-X. These missions require mirror assemblies that have angular resolutions $\leq$1.5". NGXO combines the stress-free nature of single-crystal silicon with advanced polishing techniques to produce mirror segments with figure quality comparable to or better than Chandra mirror shells, yet ten times thinner and therefore lighter. In 2025, NGXO was engaged in the AXIS phase A study, and the outcome of that work is summarized here, showing that the NGXO technology has made substantial progress, obtained robust statistics on individual segment performance, and achieved the first realization of a full-scale mirror module.

Items.Authors: Victor L. Krabbendam, Sandrine J. Thomas
Items.Title: NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory construction completion status
Items.Abstract: The NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory has started Operations. The ground-based optical Observatory in Chile, with its 8.4-m telescope, a 3.2 gigapixels camera and a sophisticated data pipeline, was commissioned and construction is substantially complete. The Operations team is now preparing for the survey. In the last two years, the project has finished the system integration, commissioning, and verification. The final stages included system testing with a Commissioning Camera to capture the first photons and then full system commissioning with the main Camera. The observatory has successfully demonstrated the powerful capability of its high precision optical system, sensitive camera and superb data management system with test surveys that produced science quality data products, including a first data release, providing commissioning observations that already support scientific discovery. The project has items to close while preparations continue for survey start, beginning of 2026.

Items.Authors: Cristian Silva
Items.Title: Observing the Observatory. The Observability Journey of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory
Items.Abstract: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory is not only an observatory, it is also a distributed production engine for sci-  ence. During operations, it will move thousands of images, metadata, and alerts through the telescope, camera,  network, storage, and processing services every night. Rubin will produce up to 20 TB of raw data per night  (10TB on the wire with compression), with an alert stream that reaches millions of events and a target latency  of nearly 1 minute.  In this environment, simple monitoring is not enough. We need to ask why something changed, where latency  started, which component is under pressure, and whether the behavior is connected with the observing conditions  or the state of the facility. This paper describes the observability journey of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory  DevOps team, a multi-year effort to build, refine, and scale a modern observability stack for one of the most  ambitious astronomical facilities ever constructed.

Items.Authors: Lauren Schatz, Mark L. Eickhoff, Robert L. Johnson, Marjorie A. Guruléx, Sarah Strickland, Gregory Smith, Tanya Tavenner, Leonard Gurule, Steven Massey, Jeff W. Richey, Frank Lison, Armin Zach, Martin Enderlein, Sebastian Hepp
Items.Title: On-sky testing results of the world’s brightest 75 W sodium beacon
Items.Abstract: The current generation of sodium laser beacons are 22 W in power and excite the main sodium D2A using 589 nm light. Starfire Optical Range is testing and characterizing the performance of the newest generation of laser beacons on-sky. The “Wolpertinger” sodium laser is a 75 W, 589 nm laser developed by Toptica Projects. This laser uses single sideband repumping to pump the D2B line efficiently. In addition, this laser can frequency “chirp”, by doppler shifting the laser frequency in a sawtooth pattern to prevent saturation of sodium atoms when using high powered lasers. In this presentation we discuss results of the Wolpertinger taken from over six weeks of on-sky observations at Starfire Optical Range. Included in these results, we report a 3.6x increase in brightness from an experiment directly comparing the Wolpertinger laser with the current generation 22 W beacons.

Items.Authors: John Kelley, IceCube Collaboration
Items.Title: Operations of the IceCube Neutrino Observatory at the South Pole
Items.Abstract: The IceCube Neutrino Observatory is a cubic kilometer-scale neutrino detector at the geographic South Pole. The remote Antarctic location and constrained logistics provide several challenges to observatory operations, with no flights in or out of the site for eight months a year. Nevertheless, since the beginning of full operations in 2011, the average uptime of the detector has been over 99.6%, and the failure rate of the 5484 sensors has been less than one per year. We present our strategies for data archival and transfer, on-site maintenance, hardware sparing and upgrades, and real-time collaboration with other astronomical observatories. We will also describe our technical methods for time synchronization of the distributed sensor array. The design of IceCube-Gen2, a potential future expansion, is cognizant of the power and data bandwidth limitations of the South Pole site while taking advantage of its unique characteristics for neutrino detection.

Items.Authors: Douglas R. Gies, Nicholas J. Scott, Gail H. Schaefer
Items.Title: Recent technical and scientific highlights from the CHARA Array
Items.Abstract: The Center for High Angular Resolution Astronomy (CHARA) Array is a six-element interferometer at Mount Wilson Observatory with baselines ranging from 34 to 331 m. The Array hosts a number of new or upgraded, six-telescope beam combiners that span the spectrum from the visible R-band to the near-infrared K-band with a range in available spectral resolution. The most recent is the Silmaril combiner that is a three-telescope instrument for H- and K-bands that is designed for very high sensitivity on fainter targets. A seventh, mobile telescope is now on-site for use with fiber optics for H-band beam transport. The mobile telescope will extend the baseline range from 20 m to 579 m, creating new opportunities for measurements of stars with large and small angular diameters. Observing time is available to the community through a program funded by NSF. The observing programs are solicited and peer-reviewed by NSF's NOIRLab.

Items.Authors: David R. Andersen, Alastair Heptonstall, Kanaka Warad, Mojtaba Taheri Nieh, Michael Fitzgerald, Quinn Konopacky, James Larkin, Dimitri Mawet, Eric Peng, Charles Steidel, Ryuji Suzuki, Shelley Wright
Items.Title: The First-Light Instrument Suite at TMT: Capabilities and Status Update
Items.Abstract: The Thirty Meter Telescope (TMT) will host three first-light instruments: IRIS, WFOS, and MODHIS. IRIS is a diffraction-limited imager and integral-field spectrograph used with NFIRAOS, the TMT facility adaptive optics system, offering a 34×34 arcsec field and multiple spaxel scales at R~4000–10,000. MODHIS, also behind NFIRAOS, targets exoplanet science with single-object spectroscopy at R~100,000. WFOS is a seeing-limited optical multi-object spectrograph with an 8×3 arcmin field and the ability to observe ~100 targets at R~1500–5000.  We summarize recent progress across the TMT instrument suite, including refinements to the opto-mechanical designs, and new capabilities, along with updated performance expectations. The instruments are now advancing toward late-stage design and preparation for fabrication, integration, and verification, positioning the program to deliver a fully capable first-light instrument suite for TMT operations in the 2030s.

Bauman, William Wahl, Paul O'Connor, Françoise Virieux, Alexandre Boucaud, Camille Parisel, Éric Auborg, Eric Lagorio, Pierre Karst, Aurélien Marini, Didier Laporte, Francis Vezzu, Guillaume Daubard, Patrick Breugnon, Tim W. Waters, Merlin Fisher-Levine, Antoine Bernard, Mile Kusulja
Items.Title: The on-sky performance of the LSST Camera CCD array
Items.Abstract: The focal plane of the LSST Camera contains 189 individual science CCDs, along with 4 wavefront and 8 guider CCDs. Altogether, the LSST Camera CCDs compose the largest focal plane ever constructed. The LSST Camera is the primary instrument of Rubin Observatory, which will begin the Legacy Survey of Space and Time in 2026. In this proceeding, we describe the on-sky performance of the LSST Camera CCDs, from receipt at NSF/DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory in May 2024 to on-sky observations during the first year of operations. We discuss the process to establish functionality of several CCDs which were affected by an electrical short and faulty analog-digital converter, optimizations of readout timing in response to changes in the survey strategy, and implementation of enhanced focal plane safety measures through an active clearing mechanism on the CCDs. Finally, we discuss sensor features observed on-sky, and global performance during the first year of operations.

Items.Authors: Stacey R. Sueoka, David M. Harrington, Thomas A. Schad, Sarah A. Jaeggli, Andre Fehlmann, Tetsu Anan
Items.Title: Fringe suppression and polarization calibration at DKIST
Items.Abstract: Accurate spectro-polarimery is a critical observational tool in solar physics. At DKIST, several  large ongoing efforts are providing more accurate calibration through system-level polarization  metrology and also instrument improvement through the suppression of interference fringes  frequently corrupting solar measurements. We present advances in optical fringe-suppression  techniques to reduce fringes by orders of magnitude in DKIST instruments.   Additional custom metrology equipment for polarization calibration of DKIST has been observing the sun through the Cryo-NIRSP optical path, and is being upgraded following many lessons learned.  The NSO Coude Spectro-Polarimeter (NCSP) calibration system is combined with lab metrology  equipment outputs to create a detailed thin film coating model of the system, inform thermal  behavior of many polarization optics, and provide additional instrument filter metrology for  improving instrument quality beyond the initial construction phases.

Items.Authors: Sally Lau, Ming-Tang Chen, Ryan Chilson, Derek Kubo, Peter Oshiro, Naomi Owens, Jean-François Cliche, Andre Renard, Nina Gusinskaia
Items.Title: Back-end signal processing and operational status of the FRB Hawaiʻi outrigger station
Items.Abstract: The FRB Telescope Array in Pāhala, Hawaiʻi, serves as an outrigger station for the CHIME project, one of the worldʻs leading efforts to detect and study fast radio bursts. Operated in collaboration with the Trottier Space Institute at McGill University, the Hawaiʻi array extends CHIMEʻs observational baseline, significantly improving the ability to pinpoint the origin of these millisecond cosmic signals. The array includes ten 6-meter parabolic dishes and twelve log-periodic dipole antennas covering 400-800 MHz, supported by the ICEBoard processing engine and Python-based control software for real-time data capture and correlation. Continuous monitoring via Grafana ensures reliable 24/7 operation at this off-grid, solar powered site. Initial tests, including solar fringe on both log-periodic dipole antennas and 6-meter parabolic dishes, which demonstrated the arrayʻs stability and readiness to deliver high quality data to the CHIME network.

Items.Authors: Martin Pertenaïs, Till Hagelschuer, Gisbert Peter, Ingo Walter, Simone del Togno, Yaquelin M. Rosas-Ortiz, Andrei Cacovean, Karsten Westerdorff, Alexander Fitzner, Emanuel Kopp, Giulia Alemanno, Nils Müller, Ana-Catalina Plesa
Items.Title: Challenges in designing and developing an instrument for two space agencies simultaneously
Items.Abstract: VEM and VenSpec-M are two nearly identical near-infrared pushbroom spectrometer developed at the DLR Institute of Space Research for the VERITAS (NASA/JPL) and EnVIsion (ESA) missions to Venus.     This exercise aims to provide an overview of the enriching experience acquired during the past years in designing and developing a specialized instrument for the same planet, with similar and complementary science goals, same physical laws, nearly same launch period, and yet sometimes very different design standards, development philosophies, operations and interface requirement provided by the two different stakeholders (ESA and JPL).    This is meant as a platform for the community to learn from others, and understand that most of the time, there is no unique right way. Several paths can lead to the same result: a successful mission.

Items.Authors: Joseph M. Colosimo, Kristin K. Madsen, Kai-wing Chan, Tabatha DeVita, Naoko Hamaguchi, Michal Hlinka, Steve Kenyon, Richard Koenecke, James Mazzarella, Ai Numata, Takashi Okajima, Jessica Patel, Raul E. Riveros, Marton Sharpe, Keisuke Tamura, Jonathan Tsang, Youwei Yao, William W. Zhang
Items.Title: Characterizing segmented silicon optics for future X-ray observatories
Items.Abstract: Future X-ray mission concepts aim to provide much greater sensitivity than that achieved by current or past missions. The X-ray mirror assemblies on these missions will require optics that provide high angular resolution and large collecting areas, requiring mirrors to be lightweight and cost-effective to produce. The Next-Generation X-ray Optics group at Goddard Space Flight Center is developing segmented mono-crystalline silicon optics to meet these requirements.    Precise characterization of mirror surfaces over a wide range of spatial scales is essential to the development of these optics. We discuss the metrology techniques used to characterize mirror figure and finish, their application in mirror fabrication, and the simulation techniques used to estimate mirror performance based on these measurements. Additionally, we validate our multi-scale predictive models by comparing the simulated optical performance directly against X-ray beamline measurements of a test module.

Items.Authors: Nicolas Reyes, Andrey Baryshev, Gerrit Grutzeck, Christopher Heiter, Sebastian Jorquera, Attila Kovacs, Dennis Koopmans, Lingyu Wang, Axel Weiss, Vicente Woolvet, Stephen Yates, Jochem Baselmans
Items.Title: The AMKID camera at the APEX telescope: overview of the 2024-2025 verification campaign
Items.Abstract: The APEX Microwave Kinetic Inductance Detector (AMKID) camera is a dual-color wide field-of-view camera based on kinetic inductance detectors installed at the 12-meter APEX telescope. Performing a large number of pixels (13.952 detectors in the 350um band and 3.520 detectors in the 870um band) it is expected to make a significant contribution in different areas of submillimeter astronomy. In this article we present the current status of the instrument and the first results of the science verification campaign performed in 2024 and 2025.

Items.Authors: Aoi Takahashi, Naoki Isobe, Shingo Kashima, Ryou Ohsawa, Ryohei Kano, Hirokazu Kataza, Fumihiko Usui, Iona Kondo, Takehiko Wada, Yoshiyuki Yamada, Koichi Takeda, Yukina Arima
Items.Title: Validation of the image-distortion robustness to thermal deformation of the JASMINE telescope
Items.Abstract: We are promoting conceptual design and the validation study of the telescope on board the Japan Astrometry Satellite Mission for INfrared Exploration (JASMINE). Precise correction of image distortion, which is a key technical challenge for astrometry, may be complicated by the time variation of point spread function centroids caused by thermal deformation of the telescope due to changing thermal condition in orbit. To assess this effect, we conducted a Structural Thermal Optical Performance analysis.   After correcting image shifts and magnification changes, the time variation of the distortion in the second or higher orders was found to be approximately 1 nm RMS, corresponding to 50 μarcsec RMS in position angle. The time stability is insufficient to achieve the mission requirement of annual parallax estimation with a precision better than 40 μarcsec. This demonstrates the necessity of the correction of time-varying distortions in the second order during post processing.

Items.Authors: Konstantin B. Holzner, Armin Zach, Georg Heinze, Sebastian Hepp, Manuel Brekenfeld, Philipp Putzer, Bernward Dimke, Tobias Mayer, Alexander Niggebaum, Bernhard Ernstberger, Martin Enderlein, Frank Lison
Items.Title: A new versatile guide star laser platform
Items.Abstract: Sodium guide star lasers have become a workhorse in ground-based astronomy and promise compelling benefits for emergent applications such as uplink satellite communications and laser-based space debris maneuvering. With lessons learned from 10 years of operation at large-scale astronomy facilities, we have developed the next-generation laser platform to support the entire breadth of applications. Thanks to its modularity, it combines highest reliability with flexibility for customized configurations. The standard product delivers up to 50 W of single-frequency output at 589 nm with single-sideband repumping and additional optimizations for a maximally efficient excitation of sodium atoms. Targeting advanced applications such as AO correction in the visible and tip/tilt determination with a polychromatic laser guide star, we have demonstrated record output powers of >145 W via coherent beam combination, as well as a new emission wavelength at 569 nm for two-step sodium excitation.

Items.Authors: Keito Kurashima, Shigeyuki Sako, Kazuya Matsubayashi, Hidenori Takahashi, Sohei Kondo, Katsuhiro Murata, Miho Kawabata, Kenta Taguchi
Items.Title: Characterization and on-sky evaluation of a large-format SPAD image sensor for astronomy
Items.Abstract: We report the results of laboratory characterization and on-sky evaluations conducted with a large-format Single Photon Avalanche Diode (SPAD) image sensor for astronomical observations. This sensor is an avalanche photodiode (APD) array, with quenching circuits and digital counters arranged directly beneath each individual pixel. This structure allows counting pulse signals generated by single-photon avalanche events on each pixel. This natively digital operation realizes zero readout noise. We evaluated a prototype SPAD image sensor (2072×1548 pixels, 6.4 µm size) in laboratory and on-sky tests. The results confirmed excellent performance, including good linearity, Poisson-compliant statistics, and low dark count rate when cooled, with readout noise and persistence below our detection limit. SPAD image sensors are expected to bring significant sensitivity improvements for low-background, high-speed imaging and high-dispersion spectroscopy.

Items.Authors: Linling Shuai, John D. Monnier, Benjamin R. Setterholm, Stefan Kraus, Narsireddy Anugu, Tyler Gardner, Jean-Baptiste Le Bouquin, Gail Schaefer
Items.Title: Dust at the extreme: polarimetric interferometry and modeling with the CHARA Array
Items.Abstract: Combining high–angular-resolution interferometry with polarimetry enables us to directly study where dust forms and where it is destroyed around stars. With MIRCX-POL, we now have a unique capability to probe the dust environments of AGB stars and young stellar objects at milliarcsecond scales across the optical and near-infrared. We have developed a framework to characterize instrumental polarization throughout the CHARA optical train, allowing accurate measurements of Stokes Q and U. Radiative-transfer models predict strong polarization signatures at the dust sublimation rim, and I will present the first preliminary long-baseline interferometric Stokes Q/U results for AGB shells and YSO disks. These full-Stokes observations can be extended to the K band with VLTI/GRAVITY in the future, and allow reconstruction of fully polarized interferometric images.

Items.Authors: Kim Hoogenberg
Items.Title: Engineering the spectrum: How ASTRON’s Rainbow team advances software-first radio astronomy
Items.Abstract: Modern radio astronomy increasingly depends on software-mediated workflows that connect scientific intent, observatory operations, data archives, and processing environments. At ASTRON, the Rainbow team contributes to this software-first transition through user-facing and data-facing systems for proposal preparation, calculation-service integration, project administration, staging, archive interaction, user data ingest, and science portal development.    Through LOFAR and LOFAR2.0-related workflow use cases, we show how coherent software engineering practices reduce operational risk, streamline complexity, and shorten time to production. Rather than treating telescope-control, archive, processing, and user-facing tools as one uniform platform, we describe overlapping software domains connected by explicit interfaces, shared frontend patterns, CI/CD, provenance, operational visibility, and support feedback loops.

Items.Authors: Ryan J. Wierckx, Tyrone Woods
Items.Title: Hybrid Remote Telescopes in the High Arctic for Astronomy and Satellite Downlink
Items.Abstract: Satellite downlink demand has never been higher, with bandwidth requirements steadily increasing, and radio bands becoming crowded, the need for high speed satellite communications is great. At the forefront of this need are IR communications. Using lasers, downlink speeds can well exceed the 1GB/s mark. Use of this technology is limited by lack of infrastructure. By developing and implementing deployable, remote operable optical telescopes in the Canadian arctic, we hope to create the necessary infrastructure to provide future satellites, notably those in sun-synchronous orbits, such as CASTOR, with high bandwidth downlink capability. Operating and protecting precision equipment in Canada’s arctic poses a challenge. Here we describe a small scale prototype developed at the University of Manitoba’s Glenlea site, which has successfully engaged in remote operations throughout the cold Winnipeg winter, and initial progress towards deploying in the high arctic.

Items.Authors: Sebastiaan Y. Haffert, Rico Landman, Yinzi Xin
Items.Title: Quantum-optimal instruments for high-contrast imaging with multi-plane light converters
Items.Abstract: Spatial Mode Demultiplexers (SPADE) are devices that split an incoming wavefront into a particular set of electric field modes. SPADEs have been shown to be quantum-optimal for many measurement problems including coronagraphy, wavefront sensing and interferometric (nulling) beam combiners. We will show how quantum optimal SPADEs can be implemented using Multi Plane Light Converters (MPLC). MPLCs are devices that use several phase plates in sequence to achieve arbitrary unitary transformations. The phase plates themselves are implemented using liquid-crystal technology that allows us to create high-quality broadband phase plates. The accurate control of the local phase through the direct write method results in MPLCs with minimal background scatter. We will show the designs and simulated performance for each of the proposed use cases for the ELT-PCS, HWO and LIFE and show how they improve over current concepts.

Items.Authors: R. Millan-Gabet, G. Rahmer, R. A. Bernstein, A. Souza, P. H. Silva, Igor Petrucci, A. Szentgyorgyi, D. Fabricant, R. A. S. Ribeiro, R. Sharp, G. N. Mace, S. Lee, J. Lawrence, J. Crane, J. Males, L. Close, R. Simcoe, Gustav M. Pettersson, M. Cox, G. Brossus, H. Chiquito, B. Walls, R. Conan, F. Aguayo, A. Santana, S. Park, K.-M. Lam, C. Gottschalk, N. Juelsgaard, B. Bigelow, R. Goodrich, R. Demers, F. Quiros-Pacheco, N. Lowen, M. van Dam, B. Nemati
Items.Title: Science instruments for the Giant Magellan Telescope
Items.Abstract: We describe the development status of the first generation of science instruments for the Giant Magellan Telescope (GMT) and the very broad range of first-light capabilities that they will deliver.

Items.Authors: Takashi Miyata, Yuzuru Yoshii, Kotaro Kohno, Kentaro Motohara, Takeo Minezaki, Shigeyuki Sako, Fumi Egusa, Itsuki Sakon, Masahiro Konishi, Hidenori Takahashi, Takafumi Kamizuka, Kazuya Matsubayashi, Hiroaki Sameshima, Kana Morokuma-Matsui, Mitsuyoshi Yamagishi, Masataka Imai, Takashi Horiuchi, Yuki Hirao, Natsuko Kato, Kosuke Kushibiki, Leonardo Bronfman, Maria T. Ruiz, Mario Hamuy, Rene Mendez, Guido Garay, Andres Escala, Patricio Rojo
Items.Title: The University of Tokyo Atacama Observatory 6.5m telescope: project status 2026
Items.Abstract: The University of Tokyo Atacama Observatory (TAO) is an infrared-optimized telescope project promoted by the University of Tokyo. The summit facility has been completed in 2024 and is now operational. A coating system for the telescope mirrors has also been installed in the summit support building. The telescope mount was fabricated in Japan and is currently being assembled at the summit.  The first-generation instruments, MIMIZUKU, NICE, and SWIMS are undergoing final adjustments in Japan. Development of the second-generation instruments, TARdYS and Laguna, have also started.

Items.Authors: Alireza Vafa, Alireza Basohbat Novinzadeh, Amirhossein Kermani
Items.Title: A co-design framework for architecting distributed space telescopes and satellite systems
Items.Abstract: Co-designing architectures for distributed satellite systems (DSS) is increasingly critical as missions rely on constellations, formations, swarms, and fractionated spacecraft. This paper introduces a "Mission-Topology-System" (MTS) co-design framework that links mission objectives, multi-satellite configuration, and system-level technologies through an explicit iterative co-design loop for early Phase 0/A and MBSE workflows. The framework is instantiated on high-precision astronomy DSS and examined via cross-mission conformity analysis, revealing how extreme performance requirements drive tightly constrained topologies and stringent system architectures that feed back to reshape feasible mission concepts. The MTS perspective supports more structured early trade spaces and more coherent requirement flowdown for next-generation distributed space telescopes and satellite systems.

Items.Authors: Jake A. McCoy, Randall L. McEntaffer, Ross C. McCurdy, Bridget O'Meara, Alexandra N. Higley, James H. Tutt, Fabien Grisé, Gavid Girou, Nicolas M. Barrière, Maximilien J. Collon, Ramses Gunther, Alex Bayerle, Aniket Thete, Jeroen Haneveld, Bart Schurink, Mark Olde Riekerink, Mathijs Bosman, Marc A. Verschuuren, Manuel Paans, Benjamin Donovan
Items.Title: Advances in silicon pore gratings for x-ray spectroscopy
Items.Abstract: Silicon pore grating (SPG) technology is an approach to constructing modular arrays of reflection gratings for x-ray spectroscopy. Leveraging from silicon pore optic technology used for NewAthena, prototypical SPGs are currently in development for the Off-Plane Grating Rocket Experiment. Dicing processes have demonstrated success in manufacturing ribbed grating plates from nanoimprinted resist on silicon flats. Using an electron-beam written master template with un-patterned lanes that match the rib layout, these grating replicas are produced in an inorganic sol-gel resist through substrate conformal imprint lithography. With recent experiments showing that the quality of the un-patterned lanes of resist prevents direct bonding to the silicon ribs, alternative approaches to the plate-production process are under consideration. This presentation details advances made in SPG technology, including explorations of bonding to metal-coated gratings, and the use of wedged glass substrates.

Items.Authors: Eve M. Vavagiakis, CCAT Collaboration
Items.Title: CCAT: the Prime-Cam Instrument for the Fred Young Submillimeter Telescope - overview and status
Items.Abstract: Prime-Cam is a first-generation science instrument for the CCAT project’s six-meter aperture Fred Young Submillimeter Telescope (FYST), under construction at 5600 m on Cerro Chajnantor in Chile’s Atacama Desert for first light in 2026. Prime-Cam will deliver over ten times greater mapping speed at submillimeter wavelengths than current facilities for unprecedented broadband and spectroscopic measurements in windows between 1.4 – 0.3 mm (220 – 850 GHz). With Prime-Cam, CCAT will address a suite of science goals, from Big Bang cosmology, to star formation and galaxy evolution over cosmic time. Prime-Cam is scheduled for integration in FYST in 2026, with early science observations to follow. We discuss the design and in-lab cryogenic testing of the 1.8 m diameter Prime-Cam receiver with cold stages at 80 K, 40 K, 4 K, 1 K, and 100 mK, including integration with its first independently optimized instrument modules, and give an update on deployment status.

Items.Authors: John D. Monnier, James Cutler, Akshat Dubey, Bradley Bialke, Caden Burkhardt, Hannah Cherry, Raven St. Clair, Michael Meyer, Jacob Klingler, Shivani Sunil, Daniil Voloshin, Simone D’Amico, Antonio Rizza, Ethan Foss, Samuel Y.W. Low, Prachet Jain, E. Glenn Lightsey, Althea Noonan, Leonid Pogorelyuk, Melissa Flores, Albert Ostoja-Starzewski, Gautam Vasisht, Kerri Cahoy
Items.Title: Starlight acquisition and reflection toward interferometry (STARI) mission
Items.Abstract: We introduce the NASA-funded mission STARI (STarlight Acquisition and Reflection toward Interferometry), a two-spacecraft technology demonstrator for future long-baseline interferometers. STARI will perform, to our knowledge, the first in-space transfer of starlight between free-flying spacecraft, a critical step toward kilometer-scale missions. Two propulsive 8U CubeSats in low Earth orbit will fly in formation with separations up to 100 m: one relays a narrow stellar beam to the other, where an off-axis parabola reimages it into a single-mode fiber. Using differential GPS, visible LED beacons, and fast-steering mirrors in closed loop, we aim to sustain diffraction-limited, high-throughput fiber coupling during formation flight. STARI, targeting launch in 2029, is designed to retire key optical and control risks for missions such as the Large Interferometer for Exoplanets (LIFE) that seek to detect atmospheric biomarkers on nearby Earth-like exoplanets.

Items.Authors: Albert Wai Kit Lau, Sebastián Manosalva, Gonzalo Burgos, Bruno Pollarolo, Tomas Cassanelli, Ricardo Finger, Juan Mena-Parra, Keith Vanderlinde
Items.Title: System architecture and deployment of the CHARTS pathfinder wide-field radio transient interferometer
Items.Abstract: The Canadian-Chilean Array for Radio Transient Studies (CHARTS) is a wide-field, low-frequency radio interferometer under construction located in Laguna Carén, Santiago, Chile, dedicated to detecting Fast Radio Bursts and other cosmic transients in the southern sky. Designed for high-impact science at a sustainable cost, CHARTS combines custom antenna technology with efficient commercial electronics. This presentation details the deployment and commissioning of the CHARTS Pathfinder, a technological testbed that demonstrates the instrument's end-to-end performance and validates the path toward the full observatory.

Items.Authors: S. Serafini, E. de Muri, M. Scrinzi, D. Wei, N. Guo, W. Clements
Items.Title: High-power RFA-based 589-nm guide star laser with enhanced non-resonant frequency doubling
Items.Abstract: A novel approach for high-power 589-nm Guide Star Laser is presented: it is based on the well-established technology of narrow-band Raman Fiber Amplifier, pushed to an unprecedented output power level, and an innovative technique for frequency doubling. This technique uses non-resonant non-linear crystal doubling stages with a conversion efficiency comparable to state-of-the-art resonant doublers. The system natively supports any spectral engineering of the radiation. This novel approach permits a simple, scalable and cost-effective system.

Items.Authors: Brian J. Henderson, James Throckmorton, Matthew East
Items.Title: Polarization effects in meter-scale coatings
Items.Abstract: Imaging terrestrial exoplanets with meter-scale optics faces challenges due to contrast degradations caused by non-uniform thin film coatings. Specifically, high-angle deposition can lead to structured crystals that produce localized optical transparency for specific polarizations. This study aims to characterize structured crystal growth in meter-scale depositions for materials relevant to the Habitable Worlds mission, conduct physics-based modeling to characterize structured thin film birefringence, and apply findings in a system-level polarization ray trace analysis.

Items.Authors: Kenneth W. Lin, Abby Bault, Julien Guy, Patrick Jelinsky, Armin Karcher, Claire Poppett, Vamsi Vytla
Items.Title: Characterization of a large format MAS CCD for DESI Run 2
Items.Abstract: Ultra-low-noise, fast-readout detectors are essential for photon-limited spectroscopy of Earth-like exoplanets and faint, high-redshift galaxies. Multi-amplifier sensing (MAS) CCDs, developed jointly by Berkeley Lab and Fermilab, have been experimentally shown to achieve sub-electron noise while maintaining readout speeds comparable to detectors used in state-of-the-art spectrographs such as those in the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI). These devices employ chains of “skipper” floating-gate amplifiers along the serial register, enabling repeated, non-destructive, statistically independent charge measurements. We present the motivation for the DESI-2 blue CCD upgrade. We report initial characterization results of new blue-optimized 4k×4k, 128-channel MAS CCDs (STA 5500) designed for the DESI-2 spectrograph upgrade. We describe the infrastructure we have developed for instrumenting this large-format device, including new readout electronics supporting differential readout.

Items.Authors: Andrew T. Cenko, Tim Buschmann, Marc A. Murison, Barry S. Rothberg, Stephen J. Williams
Items.Title: Customizable, Reactive, and Adaptive Automated Observing
Items.Abstract: Planning and scheduling telescope observations is a complicated process, particularly for long-term and/or distributed observational programs. Adapting to local conditions, such as astronomical seeing and weather, while still achieving project goals requires careful analysis, planning, collaboration, and execution. With ever increasing computer power available, more of this process can be automated. The USNO's unified telescope control software includes a highly customizable observing structure expandable by inheriting from a base Python observing program class. We discuss the structure of this class, how subclasses can inherit and expand on this base functionality, and how this structure allows for managing long-term observing programs, adapting to local conditions, interacting with distributed systems, and reacting to transient events. We also discuss how this structure can work within manual, semi-automated, and fully automated observing schemes.

Items.Authors: Kevin Barjot, Aline Dinkelaker, Nic Scott, Aurélien Benoït, Narsireddy Anugu, Alyssa V. Mayer, Jacopo Siliprandi, Robert R. Thomson, Kalaga Madhav, Gail Schaefer, Lucas Labadie
Items.Title: First on-sky fringes in K-band of an ULI-manufactured integrated optics beam combiner at the CHARA observatory
Items.Abstract: NIR long-baseline interferometric observations reach angular resolutions on the order of milliarcseconds which opens science cases such as exozodiacal dust of early-type main sequence stars at the CHARA array. Integrated-optics technologies bring a compact footprint which reduces the instrument sensitivity to its environment. Following the decommissioning of JouFLU, the CHara ARray Integrated Optics Testbench (CHARIOT) aims to implement a plug-and-play platform to easily test and characterise innovative technologies of integrated-optics beam combiners in K-band. Currently, CHARIOT integrates a proof-of-concept 2-T fiber-connectorised integrated-optics beam combiner manufactured using the ultrafast laser-inscription fabrication technique. This talk gives an update on the CHARIOT development, and presents its first on-sky results. CHARIOT is able to correctly detect on-sky fringes at a limiting-star magnitude of K-band = 5.2, and reach a sub-1% visibility precision for Kmag = 2.

Items.Authors: Jan David Mol, Hannes Feldt, Reinder Kraaij, Corné Lukken
Items.Title: LOFAR 2.0: constructing a secure, scalable, and automated telescope using open source and open protocols
Items.Abstract: If you want to do a great job, you need to do it twice! We are fortunate that we have that chance while building a new software infrastructure to operate LOFAR 2.0, the successor of the Low Frequency Array that operated for 10 years, designed to process 1 Tbit/s of aggregated antenna data.    In LOFAR 2.0, we create a software stack of off-the-shelf open-source software which provides us with a low-cost yet highly modular landscape. It provides a integrated solution, in which our operators get a uniform view across both the software and hardware of our telescope, developers can dynamically deploy, and system admins can easily expand.

Items.Authors: Ben Keller
Items.Title: CCAT: design and characterization of the 350 GHz Instrument Module
Items.Abstract: The CCAT Collaboration’s Prime-Cam instrument will soon be deployed to the Fred Young Submillimeter Telescope (FYST) in Chile’s Atacama Desert. Featuring prominently in Prime-Cam’s calibration and early science observations will be the 350 GHz “instrument module”, which will field more than 10,000 broadband microwave kinetic inductance detectors (MKIDs) across 3 detector arrays. Forecasts show this instrument module will be capable of making the most sensitive yet measurements of polarized dust emission, with the potential to reduce bias and thereby improve constraints on the tensor-to-scalar ratio r, while also enabling new galactic polarization science. In this paper we discuss the design of the 350 GHz instrument module, covering aspects of the detectors and readout, optics, thermal budget, and mechanical considerations. We then report on the results of in-lab testing and validation of the instrument performed prior to its shipment to the telescope site in Chile.

Items.Authors: Amanda C. Santana, Igor Petrucci, Hebert Costa, Francisco Aguayo, Brian Walls
Items.Title: Digital systems engineering framework for the Giant Magellan Telescope: integrating requirements, interfaces, and configuration management
Items.Abstract: The Giant Magellan Telescope (GMT) is entering its final design stage. To manage the project’s complexity, GMT developed an innovative digital systems engineering framework that integrates advanced software tools and AI. This unified platform connects requirements, interfaces, and configuration data across all engineering disciplines, improving collaboration and efficiency. The system is built on the IBM Engineering Lifecycle Management (ELM) suite, with complementary tools for data analytics, configuration-management integration and automated reporting. The environment has increased engineering efficiency, reached near-complete traceability coverage, cut document-generation effort by up to 66.5% and improved requirements quality by 33.7%. By combining digital engineering with AI-driven quality analysis, GMT is establishing a new model for traceability, design integrity, and teamwork,laying the foundation for successful verification, validation, and future observatory operations.

Items.Authors: Isshin Nagataka, Hatsune Goto, Daisuke Yonetoku, Daiki Ishi, Yoshitomo Maeda, Hsien-Chieh Shen, Ryuji Kondo, Akito Kutsumi, Hiroshi Tomida, Makoto Arimoto, Shutaro Ueda, Tatsuya Sawano, Keito Watanabe, Haruaki Niinuma, Takumi Togashi, Rinon Kageyama, Tatsuro Kanenaga, Tenshin Otsuka, Junpei Kuwabara, Motoko Serino, Yuta Yamamoto, Kanta Yagi, Kaita Nakahashi, Kenta Kanou, Satoshi Sugita, Yuya Nagase, Naoki Takase, Shunichi Nakatsubo, Shuichi Gunji, Akihiro Doi, Hideo Matsuhara, Toru Kaga
Items.Title: Imaging performance evaluation of the Lobster Eye optics aboard HiZ-GUNDAM satellite
Items.Abstract: HiZ-GUNDAM is a satellite mission aimed at exploring the early Universe by observing gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), one of the most energetic explosive phenomena in the universe.  The Wide-Field X-ray Monitor(EAGLE) onboard this satellite collects X-rays using Lobster eye optics and detects them using a focal plane image sensor as pnCCD.This detector provides a field of view of 0.53 sr in the soft X-ray band and aims to determine the incident direction of GRBs with an accuracy better than 1.5 arcmin (1σ).  The Lobster Eye optics use multiple Micro Pore Optics (MPOs) arranged on a spherical surface to achieve a wide field of view.   In this study, we evaluated its astronomical performance through an X-ray beam experiment using the 27-m beamline at the Institute of Space and Astronautical Science (ISAS).  In this presentation, we report on the calibration results of the angular response used to determine the X-ray incident direction, as well as the spatial dependence of the effective area.

Items.Authors: Deborah Busonero, Alberto Riva, Mario Gai, Alessandro Sozzetti, Matteo Pinamonti, Mauro Focardi, Pierpaolo Merola, Vladimiro Noce, Jesper Skottfelt, David Hall, Daniele Gallieni, Alberto Vecchiato, Ummi Abbas, Marcello Agostino Scalera, Fabrizio Fornasiero, Chiara Scandaglia, Marina Vela Nuñez, Simone Chiarucci, Alessandro Grasso
Items.Title: OCEAN: a space telescope for Orbit Characterization of near-by Exoplanets by Astrometric determinatioN on a cubesat enviroment
Items.Abstract: The paper presents the current status and technological advancements of OCEAN (Orbit Characterization of near-by exoplanetary systems by Astrometric determinatioN) mission. The mission is conceived as a 36 U Cubesat, aiming at rapid implementation with a compact telescope designed for high stability and low sensitivity to perturbations, ensuring 1-μas systematic floor. The payload relies on a single-aperture, highly-stable space telescope enforcing circular symmetry on the whole optical system, down to the detector populating an annular region of uniform diffraction limited imaging. The payload is compact, light, and cheap. OCEAN represents a transformative step toward democratizing space-based based astrometry and exoplanet discovery. The mission combines scientific ambition with engineering pragmatism. It builds on existing CubeSat heritage while pushing the limits of precision and stability, potentially unlocking a new class of affordable, targeted astronomical observatories.

Items.Authors: Shaunel M. Walker, Stanley Kuja, Timothy Molteno
Items.Title: Optimization of the TART spiral array configuration for enhanced u-v coverage for low-cost radio interferometry
Items.Abstract: Radio interferometry requires antenna arrays with good electromagnetic characteristics and adequate u-v coverage. The Transient Array Radio Telescope (TART) project provides affordable, open-source radio astronomy instrumentation using patch antenna arrays operating at 1.575 GHz for interferometric applications. The TART instruments deployed in most partner countries primarily use the spiral array configuration, which is not formally optimized using scientific optimization methods. This paper presents a multi-criteria Differential Evolution optimization of the spiral array configuration, balancing u-v coverage (45%), shape preservation (35%), and baseline diversity (20%), subject to a ±0.15 m position constraint for hardware compatibility. The optimization yields a 1.0 percentage point gain in the u–v filling factor, from 58.8% to 59.8%, establishing the 5-arm spiral as near-optimal within the TART platform constraints and providing a reference for future deployments.

Items.Authors: Jean-Tristan M. Buey, Sylvestre Lacour, Mathias Nowak, Elsa Huby, Jean-Luc Gach, Matthew Hicks, Derek Ives
Items.Title: Presentation of the design and first results of large format APD infra-red detector at Leonardo and camera at FLI for the PLANETES project
Items.Abstract: The PLANETES project, funded by the ERC, aims to design and build a new spectrometer for the VLTI (ESO), integrated a near-infrared camera (J band) equipped with a large-format 2k × 2k detector operating in photon-counting mode with APD pixels. The detector is developed by Leonardo and will be integrated inside a camera designed by First Light Imaging.  The very demanding scientific requirements will be presented, the camera must work in photon counting mode, dealing with very bright objects (stars) and faint objects (planets).  We will present initial detector-characterization results, the selection criteria for choosing devices from the Leonardo production batch, and the overall camera design.

Items.Authors: Stuart McMuldroch, Roberta Zanin, Volker Heinz, Bernard Lopez, Andrea Cremonini, Markus Gaug, Igor Oya, Stefan Schlenstedt, Stefano Stanghellini, Nadia Defrancesco
Items.Title: The Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory (CTAO): development status and the path to first light
Items.Abstract: The Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory (CTAO) is the next-generation facility for very-high-energy (20 GeV to 300 TeV) gamma-ray astronomy, with two observation sites in La Palma (Spain) and the Paranal desert (Chile), hosting 13 and 53 imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes (IACTs), respectively. The CTAO is now in the construction phase – four large size telescopes are in final integration on La Palma, and in Chile major infrastructure construction is ongoing and the first small and medium sized telescopes are being installed. These initial telescopes form sub-arrays of the final configuration and will start delivering data within the next two years. Software development is ongoing that provides the required array control and data processing functionality. Even at this early stage, these sub-arrays will outperform existing facilities. From now until final completion in 2031, the observatory will increase in capability as it integrates new telescopes and matures software.

Items.Authors: Jared R. Males, Laird M. Close, Sebastiaan Y. Haffert, Olivier Guyon, Victor Gasho, Douglas M. Kelly, Adam Fletcher, John Ford, Tommy Salanski, Maggie Kautz, Olivier F. Durney, Jamison Noenickx, Logan Pearce, Jay Kueny, Alycia Weinberger, Joseph D Long, Eden McEwen, Katie Twitchell, Joshua Liberman, Tiffany Nguyen, Adam Kraus, Jason Wang, Parker Johnson, Miles Lucas, Elena Tonucci, Rico Landman
Items.Title: The final design of GMagAO-X: high-contrast imaging at first-light of the GMT
Items.Abstract: GMagAO-X will be the first-light high-contrast imager on the 25 m Giant Magellan Telescope. The driving science case for GMagAO-X is characterization of the atmospheres of nearby rocky exoplanets such as Proxima Centauri b. This, and many more science cases will be enabled by a 21,000 actuator extreme adaptive optics (ExAO) system, an integrated coronagraphic wavefront control system with dedicated deformable mirrors, and a suite of imagers and spectrographs. GMagAO-X is on track to be ready at first-light of the GMT in the mid 2030s. We will provide an updated overview of the instrument designed to achieve our ambitious performance targets and the resultant expected scientific yield. We will discuss the results of risk reduction activities and prototyping. We will also briefly review progress towards demonstrating scaled performance targets with the recently commissioned MagAO-X on the 6.5 m Clay Telescope.

Items.Authors: Michel Tallon, Clémentine Béchet, Isaac Dinis, Florian Ferreira, Paul Fontanillas, Nicolas Galland, Charles Goulas, Markus Kasper, Caroline Kulcsár, Jalo Nousiainen, Henri-François Raynaud, Isabelle Tallon-Bosc, Éric Thiébaut, Maud Langlois, Anthony Boccaletti, Emiliano Diolaiti, Raphaël Galicher, Miska Le Louarn, Magali Loupias, Johan Mazoyer, Julien Milli, Laura Schreiber, Fabrice Vidal, Gaële Barbary, François Wildi
Items.Title: SAXO+, the second-stage adaptive optics for SPHERE: a review of six selected control algorithms and the results achieved to date
Items.Abstract: SAXO+ is the second-stage adaptive optics (AO) system to be inserted in cascade after SPHERE extreme AO at the VLT, aiming to improve coronagraphic contrast closer to the star and enable observations of fainter, redder stars. This leads to the use of a modulated pyramid wavefront sensor and a twice as fast AO loop. A classical optimal modal-gain integrator is the baseline control algorithm. We test five alternative algorithms offering prediction to mitigate delay, improved reconstruction, or better tolerance to PyWFS non-linearities. Three are based on linear estimation methods (Linear Quadratic Gaussian, data-driven, and iterative minimum-variance reconstructor) and two use neural networks and reinforcement learning (Policy Optimization for AO and Dual-stage Supervised & Reinforcement Learning). So all employ machine learning. Algorithms are compared with the COMPASS simulator, modeling two cascaded AO. On-sky tests with the RTC COSMIC will validate final performance and operability.
